reason: The sources provide multi-site verified details on the discovery, lopsided morphology, companion interaction, and supernovae of NGC 772.
story: Deep in the constellation Aries sits NGC 772, an enormous spiral galaxy spanning up to twice the size of the Milky Way. First cataloged by William Herschel in 1785, NGC 772 defies classic cosmic symmetry. Instead of balanced pinwheel arms, it features a radically lopsided shape resembling an apostrophe, dominated by a single, overdeveloped spiral arm. The culprit behind this strange distortion is NGC 770, a small dwarf elliptical satellite galaxy orbiting nearby. Gravitational tidal forces from NGC 770 have dragged and stretched NGC 772's galactic disk, compressing massive streams of gas and dust. This gravitational tug-of-war turned the runaway arm into a furious stellar nursery teeming with newborn blue stars. The sheer pace of star birth in this warped system became impossible to miss in 2003, when two massive stars exploded as Type II supernovae just seven weeks apart.
angle: A dwarf satellite galaxy gravitationally bullied a galaxy twice the size of the Milky Way, warping it into a lopsided freak with a single, runaway spiral arm.

claims.claim: NGC 772 was discovered by astronomer William Herschel on November 29, 1785.
NGC 772 is located in the constellation Aries.
NGC 772 is an unbarred spiral galaxy.
The galaxy displays an asymmetric, lopsided structure with one dominant spiral arm that is far more developed than the others.
The asymmetry and distortion of NGC 772 are caused by gravitational tidal interactions with its companion galaxy NGC 770.
The interacting companion, NGC 770, is a dwarf elliptical galaxy.
NGC 772 is cataloged alongside its companion as Arp 78 in Halton Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.
NGC 772 is significantly larger than the Milky Way galaxy.
The tidal interaction has triggered active star-forming regions and stellar nurseries within NGC 772.
NGC 772 contains abundant gas and prominent dust lanes concentrated within its primary spiral arm.
NGC 772 features a bright central nucleus.
Two Type II core-collapse supernovae, SN 2003hl and SN 2003iq, were observed in NGC 772 in the year 2003.
Supernova SN 2003hl was discovered by the LOTOSS search team.
Supernovae SN 2003hl and SN 2003iq were discovered approximately seven weeks apart.
NGC 772 has an apparent visual magnitude of roughly 10.3 to 10.6, allowing detection with moderate amateur telescopes.

disputed: Distance estimates vary between sources: S1 cites approximately 106 million light-years, S2 cites 130 million light-years, S3 places it around 116 million light-years, and S4 gives 115 million light-years; a script should state 'between 105 and 130 million light-years away'.

Diameter figures range from 160,000 light-years (S3) to 200,000 light-years (S1) and 240,000 light-years (S4); a script should simply describe it as roughly one to two times the size of the Milky Way.

Total recorded supernovae count varies because S1 lists a third event (SN 2022qze in 2022) while S3 details only the two 2003 events; a script should focus specifically on the rare 2003 pair that occurred seven weeks apart.
